etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French fable, from Latin fābula, from fārī (“to speak, say”) + -bula (“instrumental suffix”). See ban, and compare fabulous, fame. Doublet of fabula.

definitions.definition: A fictitious narrative intended to enforce some useful truth or precept, usually with animals, etc. as characters; an apologue. Prototypically, Aesop's Fables.
Any story told to excite wonder; common talk; the theme of talk.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Timothy 4:7, column 1:
quote.text: But refuſe prophane and olde wiues fables, and exerciſe thy ſelfe rather vnto godlineſſe.

quote.citation: 1842, Alfred Tennyson, “The Gardener’s Daughter; or, The Pictures”, in Poems. […], volume II, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, page 19:
quote.text: […] we grew / The fable of the city where we dwelt.

quote.citation: 1712 January 13 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “WEDNESDAY, January 2, 1711–1712”, in The Spectator, number 264; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume III, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC, page 316:
quote.text: I say it would look like a fable to report that this gentleman gives away all which is the overplus of a great fortune by secret methods to other men.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: The plot, story, or connected series of events forming the subject of an epic or dramatic poem.

quote.citation: 1695, John Dryden, A Parallel betwixt Painting and Poetry:
quote.text: For the moral (as Bossu observes,) is the first business of the poet, as being the groundwork of his instruction. This being formed, he contrives such a design, or fable, as may be most suitable to the moral;

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To compose fables; hence, to write or speak fiction; to write or utter what is not true.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii], page 111, column 2:
quote.text: He Fables not, I heare the enemie: / Out ſome light Horſemen, and peruſe their Wings.

quote.citation: 1709, Mat[thew] Prior, “An Ode, Humbly Inscrib’d to the Queen”, in Poems on Several Occasions, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC, stanza XVII, page 287:
quote.text: Vain now the Tales which fab’ling Poets tell, / That wav’ring Conqueſt ſtill deſires to rove; / In Marlbrô’s Camp the Goddeſs knows to dwell: / Long as the Hero’s Life remains her Love.

quote.citation: 1852, Matthew Arnold, Empedocles on Etna, Act II, in Empedocles on Etna and Other Poems, London: B. Fellowes, p. 50,[1]

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To make up; to devise, and speak of, as true or real; to tell of falsely; to recount in the form of a fable.

quote.text: Fabled by the daughters of memory. And yet it was in some way if not as memory fabled it. A phrase, then, of impatience, thud of Blake’s wings of excess.
